text:
Downy mildew (Peronosclerospora spp.) is described in this source as the most serious disease constraint on corn production in Cambodia, with severity varying by region and caused by more than one species in the genus (Kim et al. 2006).

Symptoms: infected plants show pale yellow-green striping running along the leaf veins from an early growth stage, along with stunted growth and poor cob development. A white, downy fungal growth can appear on the underside of leaves, especially visible in humid morning conditions. Severely infected plants may fail to produce a cob at all (sterility) or die early. The disease can be both seed-borne and airborne (spread by spores).

Management: because chemical control options are limited, resistant varieties are the primary defence (see the variety characteristics table for downy mildew resistance ratings). Additional practices: remove and destroy infected plants promptly to reduce spread; avoid continuous corn-on-corn planting in fields with a history of infection (rotate with a non-host crop); use certified, disease-free seed; and where available, fungicide-treated seed can give partial protection at the germination stage.
